reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Caused by reflux of alkaline duodenal contents, bile, and pancreatic secretions into the stomach, damaging the mucosa
Classically follows gastric surgery, particularly Billroth II reconstruction or pyloroplasty, where the pylorus no longer prevents duodenogastric reflux
Presents with persistent burning epigastric pain, bilious vomiting, and sometimes weight loss, with pain that is characteristically not relieved by acid suppression or antacids
Endoscopy shows bile pooling, mucosal erythema and oedema, and friability, chiefly around the stoma or in the gastric remnant
Histology reveals reactive (chemical) gastropathy with foveolar hyperplasia, oedema, and vasodilatation but little active inflammation
Bile-binding agents and prokinetics may help, and surgical diversion (such as conversion to a Roux-en-Y loop) is considered for severe, refractory disease
Long-standing bile reflux in the gastric remnant is associated with an increased risk of mucosal metaplasia and stump carcinoma
reference.pathophysiology: Bile reflux gastritis develops when duodenal contents rich in bile acids, lysolecithin, and pancreatic enzymes pass retrogradely into the stomach and disrupt the gastric mucosal barrier. This is most likely after operations that ablate or bypass the pyloric mechanism, allowing free duodenogastric reflux. The detergent action of bile salts injures surface epithelial cells and increases mucosal permeability, provoking a reactive (chemical) gastropathy characterised by foveolar hyperplasia, oedema, and capillary dilatation rather than a dense inflammatory infiltrate, and chronic injury predisposes to intestinal metaplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Peptic ulcer disease or recurrent stomal ulceration
Afferent loop syndrome after gastric surgery
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showing bile pooling and mucosal changes, with biopsies confirming reactive gastropathy
Helicobacter pylori testing to exclude a co-existing cause
Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scintigraphy to demonstrate enterogastric bile reflux
Gastric emptying study where delayed emptying is suspected
Cross-sectional imaging or contrast study to assess post-surgical anatomy and afferent loop
Full blood count and nutritional assessment where weight loss is present
redFlags: Progressive weight loss or a mass in the gastric remnant suggesting stump carcinoma
Intractable bilious vomiting causing dehydration or malnutrition
New dysplasia or metaplasia on surveillance biopsy of the remnant
reference.prognosis: Symptoms are often chronic and can be difficult to control medically; surgical bile diversion helps selected patients but carries its own morbidity, and long-standing reflux in a gastric remnant warrants awareness of the elevated risk of malignancy.
pitfalls: Persisting with acid-suppressing therapy that does not relieve alkaline reflux symptoms
Overlooking Helicobacter pylori or drug-induced injury as an alternative explanation
Attributing bilious vomiting to reflux gastritis when afferent loop obstruction is responsible
Neglecting surveillance for metaplasia and carcinoma in the long-term gastric remnant
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
